How often should you restring? The old rule is as many times a year as you play per week. Twice a week, twice a year.

It is a fine starting point, and a little conservative for polyester, which goes dead long before it breaks. The tell is usually not a broken string. It is when your shots start flying long and you find yourself swinging harder to get the same depth you had a month ago. That is the strings, not you.

We have been stringing racquets for 14 years and the service is mail in, so wherever you are, you can send yours to us. You pick the string and the tension when you order, and if you are not certain what suits your game, ask us before you do. That conversation is free and usually more useful than guessing off a shelf.

Two business days from arrival and it is on its way back.

Tennis and squash from $25. Racquetball and badminton from $35.

A question we get constantly: which weight?

Rough guide. If the ball already comes off your strings heavy and you generate your own pace, go heavier. 300g and up, and let the frame handle stability so you do not have to muscle it. If you play a lot of doubles, take the ball early, or you are working around an arm issue, lighter is not settling for less. It is a different tool for a different job.

The Fire line runs 260 through 305, so it is an easy family to try across without changing how the racquet feels.

posts.text:
16x19 or 18x20? The question behind half the racquet advice on the internet.

Open pattern, 16x19: fewer cross strings, so the bed moves more, bites more and launches higher. More spin, more forgiveness, more depth for free.

Dense pattern, 18x20: strings move less, ball comes off flatter and lower. Less spin, but the shot goes where you aimed it, every time.

The honest rule is that it follows your swing, not your level. Big western grip, heavy topspin, long finish? Open. Flatter, more compact, drive through the ball? Dense.

The Blade 98 V10 comes both ways at $299, which makes it a genuinely useful frame to test the question with.

18x20: https://www.racquetpoint.com/products/wilson-blade-98-18x20-v10-tennis-racquet

posts.text:
Unpopular opinion in a racquet shop: your shoes matter more than your racquet.

A frame that is slightly wrong costs you a bit of comfort. Shoes that are wrong cost you ankles, knees and the second half of your season. Court shoes are also the one piece of gear people reliably run into the ground, because the outsole still looks fine long after the midsole has stopped doing anything.

Rough test. Press your thumb into the midsole. If it does not push back, it is done, whatever the tread looks like.

Pro Staff 87, $110, and we are deep in sizes right now.

posts.text:
Nobody buys a racquet because of the throat. It is worth two minutes anyway.

That gap between the head and the handle is doing structural work. It is where a frame decides how much of the shock from an off centre ball reaches your arm, and how much it absorbs on the way through. Get it wrong and the racquet either feels dead or rattles your elbow.

It is also why two frames with identical numbers on paper can feel completely different in the hand. Weight, balance and head size are the easy part to publish. Everything that makes a racquet feel like something is harder to put on a spec sheet.

Which is the long way of saying: hit with it before you commit, and if your elbow has opinions, start with the 100UL at $279.

posts.text:
Tension, briefly, since it comes up more than anything else.

Tighter strings give you control and less power. Looser strings give you power, comfort and more dwell time on the ball. That is the whole trade.

Most people are strung tighter than they need to be, usually because someone told them a number in 2011 and they have repeated it ever since. If your arm aches and your shots land short, going down two or three pounds is free and often fixes both.

We are mail in and you pick the tension when you order. If you want a recommendation, tell us what the ball is doing and we will suggest one.

In defence of the oversize racquet.

There is a snobbery about head size that does not survive contact with actual tennis. A 111 square inch frame gives you a bigger sweet spot, more free depth and a lot more forgiveness on the days your timing is not there. Which, for most of us, is most days.

If you play doubles, if you are picking the game back up, or if you simply want more balls to come back over, the Ultra 111 will do more for your results than a tour frame you have to be perfect with.
